citeAs: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li (2025). VoiceAssistant-Eval: Benchmarking AI Assistants Across Listening, Speaking, and Viewing. arXiv:2509.22651.
creator: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li (CUHK MMLab, SenseTime Research, CPII under InnoHK)
description: VoiceAssistant-Eval is a comprehensive benchmark designed to assess AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing. It comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories, including natural sounds, music, spoken dialogue for listening; multi-turn dialogue, role-play imitation, and various scenarios for speaking; and highly heterogeneous images for viewing.
name: VoiceAssistant-Eval
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human evaluation was conducted on 10% of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B's responses (1,050 examples) across all 13 tasks. Pearson correlation coefficients between automated (gpt-oss-20b) and human evaluations ranged from 0.73 to 1.00, with an overall correlation of 0.92. Agreement rates were uniformly high (often above 90%), with several categories at 100%, and an overall agreement rate of 96.1%. Evaluation stability was assessed by repeating scoring 10 times on 10% of responses, showing narrow variance (standard deviations mostly below 3). Statistical significance testing was performed using paired two-sided t-tests with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom web-based curation tool built by the authors, which ingests candidate items with metadata, raw prompts, reference answers, and associated media (audio, images, transcripts), and allows curators to assign Good/Bad verdicts with optional notes.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A multi-stage curation process was used: (1) Deduplication using lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance to flag potential duplicates, which were manually reviewed and removed; (2) Validation to exclude incomplete or unsuitable instances (corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, incorrect answers) — approximately 10% of candidates were discarded; (3) Categorization assigning problems to 13 predefined task categories based on source metadata; (4) Sampling to balance the ratio of different tasks. A lightweight web-based curation tool was built to standardize quality checks, with curators reviewing each item and assigning Good or Bad verdicts.
rai:dataBiases: The benchmark may carry biases from its source data and design choices, as questions and contexts are drawn from academic or synthetic sources which might not reflect the full richness or fairness concerns of real deployments. The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles and associated style prompts that may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas. The monolingual English focus (except five Chinese roles) may not capture the full variability of real user interactions. The authors acknowledge that model performance on the benchmark might not fully generalize to more diverse linguistic settings.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from 47 source datasets spanning audio and visual modalities. For Listening, source data was drawn from 23 audio understanding datasets covering speech, sound, music, and general audio. For Speaking, data came from 22 datasets including 11 text datasets and 11 audio datasets, plus role profiles from RoleBench. For Viewing, MMMU was used as the source dataset, spanning 30 disciplines and 30 image formats. Text instructions were converted to audio using TTS models. 100 distinct roles were selected with 3 representative audio clips per role for role-play tasks.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data was sourced from 47 existing datasets including audio clips (natural sounds, music, speech, dialogue), images (diagrams, tables, charts, photos, etc.), and text QA pairs. Sources include LibriSpeech, Common Voice, Clotho, AudioCaps, AVQA, MusicCaps, MMMU, RoleBench, AlpacaEval, VocalBench, VoiceBench, SD-Eval, and many others. The benchmark also includes 300 role audio clips collected for role-play tasks.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset may be limited in diversity: although five Chinese roles are included in the role-play task, all other prompts and evaluations are in English, limiting generalization to diverse linguistic settings. The range of models evaluated is limited, with only one proprietary system (GPT-4o-Audio) included. The evaluation relies on automated measures and GPT-based scoring, which may introduce noise and bias. The benchmark may carry biases from source data and design choices, as questions are drawn from academic or synthetic sources. The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles that may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas. Video-audio integration and continuous audio-visual streaming tasks are not covered. The benchmark evaluates models in an offline, static manner and does not measure latency, partial utterance handling, or barge-in capabilities.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After curation, balanced sampling was applied to equalize category representation across the 13 task categories. Three TTS models (F5TTS, ChatTTS, Dia-1.6B) were used to synthesize speech instructions, with 300 role audio clips reused as prompt audio to increase speaker diversity.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text preprocessing for TTS synthesis included: (1) replacing image reference tokens (e.g., "<image1>") with descriptive phrases; (2) rewriting text using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct to make it suitable for TTS (e.g., converting mathematical expressions and numbers to spoken form); (3) rephrasing multiple-choice options for better readability. Speech synthesis used UTMOS Strong to evaluate generated speech, regenerating clips scoring below 3.8. Whisper-Large-v3 was used to transcribe synthesized audio, retaining only the sample with the lowest word error rate. In total, 13,471 high-quality speech audio files were synthesized.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark includes role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, raising concerns about identity spoofing, harassment, and fraud. To mitigate misuse risks, the authors: (i) prohibit training or releasing models intended to reproduce identifiable speakers without documented consent; (ii) require downstream users to implement consent gating and watermarking or traceability of synthetic audio; (iii) provide "safety cards" describing acceptable use, known risks, and red-team tests for voice cloning abuse. A data governance process for auditing and removal is maintained, with the right to update assets if consent or licensing concerns arise. The benchmark aims to enable research on personalization while minimizing harms related to impersonation, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics.
rai:dataUseCases: Intended for evaluating voice assistants and AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing capabilities. Specifically designed to benchmark: (1) audio understanding (natural sounds, music, speech); (2) voice personalization and speaker imitation; (3) hands-free voice interaction; (4) multimodal (audio+visual) integration; (5) spoken dialogue quality including emotion, safety, robustness, and instruction following. The dataset is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: F5TTS, ChatTTS, and Dia-1.6B (TTS models for speech synthesis); UTMOS Strong (MOS predictor for evaluating synthesized speech quality); Whisper-Large-v3 (ASR model for transcribing synthesized audio and computing WER); Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (LLM for text rewriting to improve TTS suitability); gpt-oss-20b (used as automated evaluator/judge for content quality assessment); emotion2vec (for emotion probability estimation in speaking emotion tasks); Wespeaker (for speaker similarity calculation in role-play tasks).
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes role audio clips (voice recordings) used for speaker similarity evaluation in role-play tasks. The benchmark involves voice imitation tasks that could potentially be used for identity spoofing. The authors emphasize strict consent, provenance, and anti-impersonation safeguards to address these risks.
